alt: A soil profile with O, A, B and C horizons over bedrock. Inputs of leaf litter, rain, sunlight, gases and weathered rock enter; outputs of evaporation, respiration gases, plant uptake, erosion and leaching leave. A key separates transfers such as percolation and leaching from transformations such as decomposition, humification and weathering.
caption: Leaching moves nutrients without changing them: it is a transfer, not a transformation.

alt: Close-ups of sandy soil with large particles and pores, clay soil with tiny packed particles, and loam with a mix. Rows compare them: sand drains fast but holds little water or nutrients; clay holds water and nutrients but drains slowly and waterlogs; loam combines good drainage with medium to high retention and usually has the highest productivity.
caption: Loam combines the drainage of sand with the retention of clay.

alt: A 32.0 g fresh soil sample weighs 25.0 g after oven drying (7.0 g of water lost) and 23.6 g after ignition (1.4 g of organic matter lost). Water content is 7.0 ÷ 32.0 × 100 = 21.9% of fresh mass; organic matter is 1.4 ÷ 25.0 × 100 = 5.6% of dry mass.
caption: Divide water by fresh mass but organic matter by dry mass, and say which you used.

alt: Left: salinization, where irrigation water evaporates in a hot, dry climate and leaves salts at the surface until crops cannot take up water. Right: a loss of 24.0 t per hectare per year at a bulk density of 1.2 t per cubic metre equals 2.0 mm of soil a year, or 50 mm over 25 years. Below: the six main forms of degradation.
caption: Soil is lost far faster than it forms, so degradation is hard to reverse.

alt: Three groups of methods. Slowing water or wind: contour ploughing, terracing and windbreaks. Keeping the surface covered: cover crops and mulching, reduced or no-till, controlled grazing. Maintaining organic matter and nutrients: crop rotation with legumes, compost and manure, plus lime for acidity and drip irrigation against salinization.
caption: Each method slows water or wind, covers the soil, or keeps organic matter and nutrients.

alt: One hectare of cereal gives 40 150 MJ of food energy a year. Eaten directly it feeds 10 people at 4015 MJ each a year. Fed to livestock, only about 10% (4015 MJ) passes on, feeding 1 person; the rest is lost as heat.
caption: Adding a trophic level loses about 90% of the energy, so plant-rich diets need less land.

alt: Two rows along a supply chain from field to storage, transport, shops and homes. In lower-income countries the largest losses are early, in the field, storage and transport, because of pests, poor storage and weak cold chains. In higher-income countries most waste is late, in shops and homes, because of cosmetic standards, large portions and over-buying.
caption: Poorer countries lose food early in the chain; richer countries waste it late.
